title: The needle for the next world
hookLine: tradition says Nanak gave rich Duni Chand a needle to return to him in the next world, and Duni Chand understood
tomorrow: Camp 2 close: one light, ten lamps
last: WATER FOR THE ENEMY — EVERY FACE IS HIS.

lines: THE CAR, THE WATCH, THE PHOTOS.
cards: Some people put their success on display: the car in the driveway, the watch that catches the light, the photos from the trip. In old Lahore, the story goes, a rich man named Duni Chand had a simpler system.
On the roof of his house flew a row of flags, one for every hundred thousand rupees he owned, and the whole street could count them.
One day Guru Nanak came to town, and Duni Chand invited him in, proud to host a holy man. Before he left, Nanak gave his rich host a gift. It was a needle.

teach.h: KEEP IT, AND GIVE IT BACK LATER.
teach.b: This is one of the old janamsakhi stories, the life stories of Nanak that Sikhs have told for centuries. Nanak handed Duni Chand the needle and asked a favor.
Keep this safe for me, he said, and when we meet in the next world, give it back. Duni Chand, eager to please, said of course. He took the needle to his wife and told her about the honor.
She looked at him for a long moment. And how exactly, she asked, are you going to take a needle with you when you die? That landed.
Duni Chand went straight back to Nanak. I can't do it, he said. Nothing goes with me.
Not a needle. Not the flags. Then Nanak asked him, gently, the real question.

teach.h: HOW WILL YOU TAKE A NEEDLE?
teach.b: If you can't take a needle, what will you take? The story says Duni Chand understood, and began to share what he had, giving it away to the hungry. Nanak doesn't lecture a rich man about money.
He hands him one tiny object and lets him discover the rest, with a little help from his wife. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says it plainly.
Writing of wealth, he says, in paraphrase, that many have been ruined for its sake, and that it does not go with anyone who dies. What does go?

teach.h: THE NAME, THE WORK, THE SHARING.
teach.b: Sikhs answer with the Name remembered, the honest work done, and what was shared.
The flags stay on the roof.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Duni Chand's needle to children and in talks at the gurdwara as a reminder that wealth stays behind, while remembrance, honest work and sharing go with a person.

o: a tailor who sewed robes for Guru Nanak
a Lahore governor who jailed Guru Nanak
a rich man Nanak taught with a single needle

s: Nanak scolded Duni Chand for being rich
he gave him a needle and let him discover the question himself.
it was Duni Chand's wife who saw the problem first
she asked how he planned to take a needle with him when he died.
this story is told in the janamsakhis

games.q: you're Duni Chand. a holy man asks you to keep a needle and give it back to him in the next world. your wife asks how you'll carry it there. what do you do?
o: hide the needle somewhere very safe.
go back and admit that nothing goes with you.
ask to be buried with it.
games.why: he went back to Nanak and admitted he couldn't take even a needle. the story says he understood, and began to share what he had.

practice: Pick one thing you own, your phone, a ring, a mug, a jacket, and hold it or just look at it, thinking about how you got it, what it cost, and how much it matters to you.

Then picture Duni Chand's wife asking her question: and how will you take this with you? No guilt needed; let the question sit beside the thing, then think of one thing in your life that could go with you.
